# GPU Acceleration and Parallel Pipelines


## Overview
GPU Acceleration and Parallel Pipelines refers to the family of isosurface extraction methods that offload the voxel processing, topology lookup, and geometry generation stages of the Marching Cubes algorithm to the GPU or parallel CPU architectures to achieve real-time or high-performance rendering [S1, S2, unofficial]. It solves the performance bottleneck of CPU-based immediate-mode implementations by leveraging massive parallelism [S1, unofficial]. It sets itself apart from CPU-based immediate mode implementations by leveraging massive parallelism, and from slab-based variants by processing the entire volume grid directly without explicit spatial partitioning for memory locality [G].

## Shared principles
See [Marching Cubes Lookup and Configuration](2518-marching-cubes-lookup-and-configuration.md) for the shared lookup tables and case index calculation.

## Subtopics

### [Primal Grid Marching Cubes](1211-primal-grid-marching-cubes.md)
Primal Grid Marching Cubes is a GPU-accelerated isosurface extraction technique that processes a 3D scalar volume grid using a compute shader to output a triangle mesh. It distinguishes itself from CPU-based implementations by leveraging massive parallelism to process voxels simultaneously, utilizing a fixed-size buffer with a global atomic counter and a cleanup pass to manage memory, ensuring deterministic memory usage and GPU-friendly parallelism. Unlike direct volume rendering, it produces an explicit geometric representation. Choose it when deterministic GPU memory usage and high throughput are required for large volumes.

### [GPU Marching Cubes with Histogram Pyramid](2317-gpu-marching-cubes-with-histogram-pyramid.md)
GPU Marching Cubes with Histogram Pyramid is a parallel isosurface extraction method that uses a Histogram Pyramid (HP) to count and locate surface triangles without atomic operations or sorting. It builds on [GPU Acceleration and Parallel Pipelines](4136-gpu-acceleration-and-parallel-pipelines.md) by replacing global atomic counters with a hierarchical reduction structure, enabling efficient compaction of active voxels and direct vertex placement into a Vertex Buffer Object (VBO). Unlike [GPU Marching Cubes (Compute Shader)](4687-gpu-marching-cubes-compute-shader.md), it avoids atomic contention. Choose it for high-performance rendering where atomic operations are a bottleneck.

### [CPU Immediate Mode Marching Cubes](2463-cpu-immediate-mode-marching-cubes.md)
CPU Immediate Mode Marching Cubes is a classic CPU-based surface extraction method that generates mesh vertices and normals and renders them directly via graphics API draw calls without storing a persistent mesh buffer in application memory. It serves primarily as a reference implementation for correctness and simplicity. Choose it for prototyping or when GPU memory is constrained.

### [Marching Cubes Job Scheduling](4446-marching-cubes-job-scheduling.md)
This method implements the Marching Cubes algorithm by distributing voxel chunk processing across multiple CPU threads using the Unity Job System. It solves the problem of high CPU latency in real-time terrain generation by parallelizing the lookup, vertex interpolation, and triangle assembly steps per chunk [G]. It differs from [GPU Acceleration and Parallel Pipelines](4136-gpu-acceleration-and-parallel-pipelines.md) by executing on the CPU using managed job structures rather than GPU compute shaders, and from [CPU Immediate Mode Marching Cubes](2463-cpu-immediate-mode-marching-cubes.md) by explicitly managing memory allocation via `NativeArray` and synchronization via `JobHandle` to ensure thread safety and zero-allocation during the critical path. Choose it for Unity-based terrain generation requiring CPU-side parallelism.

### [Capacity-safe slab-based Marching Cubes](4595-capacity-safe-slab-based-marching-cubes.md)
This method is a GPU-accelerated isosurface extraction pipeline that partitions the z-axis into slabs to compute exact vertex counts per slab via a two-pass strategy (classify/scan then generate), allowing for exact buffer allocation and crack-free surfaces at slab boundaries. It differs from standard Marching Cubes by resolving topological discontinuities and holes via boundary-consistent slab processing, and differs from HistoPyramids/Flying Edges by specializing counting/compaction for tightly coupled extraction, rendering, and engine integration. Choose it when crack-free boundaries and exact memory allocation are critical.

### [Capacity-Safe Marching Cubes Pipeline](4596-capacity-safe-marching-cubes-pipeline.md)
A GPU-based isosurface extraction method that avoids buffer overflow by determining the exact vertex count before geometry generation, using a two-pass approach: first computing counts/offsets, then allocating exact buffers and generating triangles. It sets itself apart from naive parallel Marching Cubes by avoiding buffer overflow and dynamic memory allocation during geometry generation through a two-pass counting and compaction strategy, building on [GPU Acceleration and Parallel Pipelines](4136-gpu-acceleration-and-parallel-pipelines.md). Unlike fixed-capacity baselines that reserve static buffers, this method determines the exact vertex count before generation, ensuring stability and preventing buffer overflow without excessive static reservation. Choose it for applications requiring strict memory bounds without atomic operations.

### [GPU Marching Cubes (Compute Shader)](4687-gpu-marching-cubes-compute-shader.md)
This method extracts an isosurface from a 3D scalar field (density texture) by executing the Marching Cubes algorithm on the GPU using a compute shader. It solves the performance bottleneck of CPU-based surface extraction by parallelizing voxel processing across thread groups. Unlike CPU immediate mode implementations, it utilizes an append buffer for dynamic triangle generation and indirect draw calls to handle variable output sizes per frame. It builds on [GPU Acceleration and Parallel Pipelines](4136-gpu-acceleration-and-parallel-pipelines.md). Choose it for general-purpose GPU-based isosurface extraction with dynamic output sizes.

### [Parallel Marching Cubes](12211-parallel-marching-cubes.md)
Parallel Marching Cubes is a parallel implementation of the Marching Cubes algorithm designed to compute isosurfaces of huge datasets that cannot fit entirely into a single machine's memory. It solves the memory bottleneck of traditional sequential Marching Cubes by using a piecewise slice strategy along the k-direction, requiring only that at least two slices fit into physical memory. Unlike siblings that assume the entire volume fits in RAM, this method distributes the workload across multiple processes or threads, enabling the processing of datasets with millions of grid values on multi-processor architectures. Choose it for out-of-core processing of massive scalar fields.

#### GPU Scalar Field Generation (Tiled Texture)
- **Definition**: Computes the scalar field values on the GPU using vertex and fragment shaders to render triangles to a tiled 2D texture [S1, unofficial].
- **Steps**: Determine tiling based on `gridSize`: 16->4x4, 32->8x4, 64->8x8, 128->8x16. Calculate `texWidth = tilesX * gridSize`, `texHeight = tilesY * gridSize` [S1, unofficial]. Create R32F texture with `CLAMP_TO_EDGE` wrapping and `NEAREST` filtering [S1, unofficial]. Bind framebuffer with `tiledTexture` as `COLOR_ATTACHMENT0` [S1, unofficial]. Set viewport to `texWidth`, `texHeight`. Pass blob parameters as `Float32Array` of size `numBlobs * 4`. Compute blob params on CPU: `pos.x = sin(i + 1.26 * time * (1.03 + 0.5*cos(0.21*i))) * 0.27 + 0.5`, `pos.y = abs(cos(i + 1.12 * time * cos(1.22 + 0.1424*i))) * 0.77`, `pos.z = cos(i + 1.32 * time * 0.1*sin((0.92 + 0.53 * i))) * 0.27 + 0.5`, `strength = 1.2 / ((sqrt(numBlobs)- 1) / 4 + 1)` [S1, unofficial].
- **Parameters**: `tilesX`, `tilesY`: number of tiles in X and Y directions, determined by `gridSize`. `texWidth`, `texHeight`: dimensions of the tiled texture [S1, unofficial].
- **Usage**: Implemented in `GpuFieldGenerator` class [S1, unofficial].

#### Incremental Chunk Re-meshing
- **Definition**: A technique to keep deformation fast and seamless by only re-meshing chunks affected by edits, rather than the entire world [S2, unofficial].
- **Steps**: Divide the world into chunks. When a dig or build operation modifies the density field, mark only the affected chunks as 'dirty'. In the `LateUpdate` phase of the frame, iterate through dirty chunks and re-mesh them using Marching Cubes [S2, unofficial].

#### Adaptive Hull Subdivision for Linearization Error
- **Steps**: Approximate the error $E_T$ for a given triangle $T$ via numerical integration over its surface. Subdivide $T$ based on the magnitude of $E_T$ to ensure error stays below a given threshold. This is done via hardware tessellation when rendering the hull mesh [S3].
- **Formula**: The linearization error at a point $p$ on the deformed surface is $E(p) = ||p - D(Dg^{-1}(p))||$, where $Dg^{-1}$ is the approximate inverse from the hull. The error over the surface of a deformed space triangle $T$ is the integral of $E(p)$ over $T$: $E_T = \int_T E(p) \, dp$ [S3].
- **Pitfall**: Increasing grid resolution in Marching Cubes to reduce triangle size scales poorly (8x more cells for double resolution) and requires regenerating the hull every frame [S3].
- **Comparison**: Unlike methods that linearize deformation over volumetric space, this method only linearizes on a 2D manifold (the hull surface), allowing easier quantification of error [S3].

## Background
The family originates from the need to accelerate the Marching Cubes algorithm, originally published by Lorensen and Cline in 1987 [10327-lookup-table-and-ambiguity-handling]. Early implementations were CPU-based. The shift to GPU acceleration began with the advent of programmable shaders and compute shaders, allowing parallel processing of voxels. Key developments include the use of append buffers for dynamic output sizes [4687-gpu-marching-cubes-compute-shader.md], histogram pyramids for atomic-free counting [2317-gpu-marching-cubes-with-histogram-pyramid.md], and capacity-safe pipelines for exact memory allocation [4596-capacity-safe-marching-cubes-pipeline.md].
